_comment: Hand corrections to the reader's output for A7, in pixels of the
full-resolution crops in .build/a7/ (see imageSize / sheetImageSize).
The reader found 136 of this board's 275 placeable designators, 49 percent --
A17 territory rather than A18's. The cause is visible on the drawing: A7's
silkscreen is dense, most labels are rotated into vertical columns two or
three characters apart (R4/R7/R5/R9 in one stack, R68/R67/R6/R8 in the next),
and the reader confuses neighbours in a column far more readily than it
invents them. Almost every drop below is a marker sitting on the label of a
designator one or two rows away in the same column.
Every one of the 136 was rendered and looked at. By tier:
agreed     63 of 69 right   (L7, Q1, R71, R75, U20 and U9 wrong)
ambiguous   4 of 11 right
single      4 of 22 right
collision  15 of 34 right
That is 86 kept and 50 dropped, and it matches what the pitfalls note predicts
for a board of this kind: agreed is the best tier, not a clean one.
All eighteen test points and both cuttable jumpers are placed by hand from a
measuring grid over drawing_full.png, whatever the reader thought. The
silkscreen convention here is a rotated label with the pad drawn as a short
bar beside it -- below the text for TP7 and TP8, above it for TP6 and TP10,
left of it for TP5, and under the text for the horizontal labels TP12, TP13,
TP16 and TP20. Every box below spans label and pad together, so a probe lands
on the eyelet and not on the lettering.
TP6 is placed even though Table 6-8 does not list it -- see the 'TP6' caveat
in a7.reference.json for the three sources that say it is real.
Nine further parts are placed by hand because they are what the procedure and
the fault codes send you to: HR2, Z1, U7, R14, K8, K9, P211, P212 and the two
jumpers.
A later pass closed the remaining gap: the 165 electrical parts the reader
never placed are now hand-placed as well, so every part with a silkscreen
designator has a board position. The designators were located with
find_in_image, the boxes measured on the drawing at full resolution, and
every one rendered back onto drawing_full.png and looked at before it landed.
Two conventions run through them: where the designator is printed inside a
component outline -- relays, DIP packages, the TO-3 and TO-220 transistors,
the inductor brackets, the boxed capacitors, R56/R85/R86 -- the marker is the
outline; where it is printed beside the part, the marker is a tight box on the
lettering.
Z4 is still deliberately unplaced: see the notOnDrawing comment below.
_layersComment: Registration of the photograph against the locator drawing, from which
build_coords.py solves the board -> photo homography. 'src' is board space
(the drawing), 'dst' is photo space; both are normalised, not pixels.
The photograph is rotated 180 degrees with respect to the drawing, and this
is the trap on this board rather than a detail: A7 is very nearly a plain
rectangle, so its outline is very nearly 180-degree symmetric and a contour
fit will settle into the wrong orientation with a perfectly respectable
residual. Four features break the symmetry and all four agree. The two DIN
connectors P211 and P212 overhang the drawing's top edge and the
photograph's bottom edge. The two ejector levers are drawn at the drawing's
bottom corners and photographed at the photograph's top corners. Three tabs
stand proud of the ejector-side edge at drawing x ~ 700 / 1500 / 2300 and at
photo x ~ 2790 / 1700 / 620 -- mirrored, in both axes. And the small notch
in the connector-side edge sits at the drawing's top-left corner (x 40-83)
and at the photograph's bottom-right. The land-on-the-part sweep at the foot
of this note is what proves it; a residual could not have.
How it was fitted. The outline was the seed, not the answer. Each straight
edge was fitted as a line over its full unobstructed run -- the
connector-side edge, the ejector-side edge, and both long sides -- the four
corners taken as the intersections of those lines, and a seed homography
solved from the four corner pairs. Masked out of those line fits: the two
DIN connector shells, which overhang the board edge in both views and hide
it (photo x 420-1490 and 1700-2820, and the matching stretches of the
drawing's top edge); the two ejector levers and the three tabs, which stand
proud of the board -- A20's levers turned out to be swung out of the
position the drawing draws them in, so they establish orientation and are
then kept out of the fit; and the drawing's own bottom edge, which the crop
5330x2860+590+450 catches at its very last rows and cannot be trusted to a
pixel.
The answer is the silkscreen. This photograph -- a7_top.jpg, which
supersedes a7_tops.jpg -- has both moulded hybrid covers off, so the
artwork is legible over nearly the whole board and there is no need to stop
at the edge, which sits a few pixels outside the plane the silkscreen is in.
The photo's yellow ink was isolated as R-B, the large yellow areas (the
Aromat relay bodies above all) opened away so that what is left is
lettering and outlines, and the photograph warped into board space through
the running fit; a 220 px patch of the drawing's own ink was then
cross-correlated against it at each of the 109 reviewed board positions and
the fit re-solved and re-matched until it stopped moving (0.2 px on the last
pass). Which peaks to believe was decided by RANSAC over all of them rather
than by agreement with the running fit, which would only have converged on
the seed; the fit shipped is then a Huber refit over every correlation, so
that the left-hand end of the drawing -- where the photograph shows the
black Q1/Q6-Q13 packages and the correlation is weakest -- is anchored
rather than thrown away by a hard threshold and spanned.
Every 'src' below is a reviewed board position already sitting in the
'board' block above, so each pair is a correspondence someone can check --
open the drawing at TP5 and the photograph at TP5 and see the same spot --
rather than a sample of a matrix. The 34 kept here are no two closer than
160 px, so they span from TP5 at the drawing's top-left corner to TP12 at
its right-hand edge and from P212 on the connector edge to TP20 and TP4 on
the ejector edge.
How good it is, measured rather than asserted. All 109 reviewed positions
were correlated; 97 of them peaked within 12 px of the whole-population fit
and are the population the answer is judged against. Against those 97 the
shipped homography lands a median 3.1 px, p90 6.4 px and worst 11.2 px out,
in pixels of the 3400 px photo the browser loads. The homography these 34
landmarks solve to agrees with the fit made to all 97 to within 3.6 px
everywhere on the board, median 1.4 px -- i.e. the landmarks reproduce the
whole-board fit rather than re-anchoring it somewhere -- and with two
independently made fits (a hard-threshold RANSAC refit, and one made with a
300 px correlation patch instead of 220) to a median 0.8 and 1.3 px.
What is left is not noise: the mean residual swings (+1.7,-2.3), (-2.0,-0.1),
(+0.3,+1.5) and (-2.0,+1.1) px across the four quarters of the board's long
axis, which is the signature of the scan of a D-size drawing rather than of
the camera, and no single projective transform removes it.
Confidence is not uniform, and the places it is thinnest are named. HR2's
moulded cover (MP6) is still fitted -- a grey moulding held by a rivet at
each end, spanning drawing x 1390-1690 -- so HR2 and the artwork under it
are the homography's word carried in from the parts around the cover rather
than a measurement. Z1, TP1 and TP17 lie just outside its edge and were each
matched on their own silkscreen. The other thin place is the drawing's
left-hand end, where the photograph shows the black Q1 and Q6-Q13 packages
and there is little yellow ink to match: TP5 and R80 anchor that end and the
correlations between them scatter about 8 px. Everything else on the board
was matched on its own artwork.
Checked the way that actually catches a bad fit, and the way a 180-degree
error could not hide from: all 109 reviewed markers were drawn onto the
photograph through this homography and looked at in tiles, end to end, from
R74, TP5 and Q24 at one end to R45, C32 and TP12 at the other. Every one
lands on its own part -- U7 on the CP82C55A, U19 on the MC1648P, U13 on the
NE522N, K8 and K9 on their Aromat relays, TP5, TP7, TP9, TP12, TP16, TP17
and TP20 each on their wire loop, and TP19 and TP3 on theirs.
One thing the sweep showed that is a placement matter and not a registration
one, recorded here so the next person does not rediscover it: the TP11 and
TP18 boxes above span their labels only, and on this board those two labels
sit about 50 px below their loops (drawing y ~ 1515 against a box centred at
1576-1580). The homography puts both boxes exactly where the drawing puts
the lettering; it is the boxes that want to be taller, the way TP5's and
TP7's are.

_dropComment: Every one of these was rendered onto the drawing and is on another part's
label. They are dropped rather than nudged, because a marker moved onto a
designator the reader never actually read is a guess wearing a measurement's
clothes -- and the coverage badge should say 49 percent if that is what it is.
The pattern is worth knowing for the next board like this one. In a rotated
column of four resistor labels the reader routinely returns the right token
and the wrong row: K5 landed on R8, K8 on R78, R9 on R79, R18 on R13, R49 on
R45, R6 on R67, R70 on R7, R71 on R11, U15 on U13, U5 on U6, U7 on U2, U20 on
Q20, U9 on the '60' of C60, L11 on the '69' of C69, C8 on the '32' of the P211
pin band. Nothing about the token is wrong; only its position is.
_notOnDrawingComment: Mechanical parts with no silkscreen designator, so they can never be placed
and counting them as unplaced would make the coverage badge lie. H1-H4 are
rivets, MP1-MP5 the TO-220 heat dissipators, MP6 the moulded hybrid cover,
MP7-MP10 the four small hi-res shields, MP11 and MP12 the nylon ejectors.
XU1 and XU2 are IC sockets: they sit under the ICs they hold and the drawing
shows the IC outline, not the socket.
Z4 is deliberately NOT here. It is an electrical part that the 1996 parts list
names and that nothing else does -- no schematic sheet, no locator position,
no Rev 9 row -- so it is left genuinely unplaced with the 'Z3 and Z4' caveat
explaining why, rather than filed away as a part that was never drawn.
_dropSchematicComment: The sheets were NOT reviewed marker by marker; there was not the budget for
379 of them. What was done instead is stated here so the next person knows
exactly what these positions are worth.
Three rules, applied together:
1. Only the 'agreed' tier is kept. The pitfalls note measures a sheet's tiers
on A14 as agreed 38/49, ambiguous 12/24, single 2/7 -- so dropping the two
weaker tiers wholesale removes most of the error without claiming a review
that did not happen. Collisions are skipped by build_coords already.
2. The legend and chart blocks go wholesale, which is where the worst of it
is. Sheet 1's TEST POINT INFORMATION box (top left, zone D8) supplied
'agreed' markers for TP2, TP6, TP7, TP8, TP9, TP10, TP19 and TP20, every
one of them pointing at a table row rather than at the net -- exactly the
failure the pitfalls note warns about, and it arrived looking like the most
trustworthy thing on the sheet. Sheet 4's legend (top right, zone D1) did
the same for TP12, TP13, TP16 and TP18. Sheet 2 is worse still: it carries
the relay bottom-view keys, the transistor package key and the relay state
chart with its five notes, and K1, K6, K7, K8, K9, K12 and K15 all arrived
in 'agreed' sitting on caption text -- rendered and confirmed by eye, which
is why sheet 2 loses two thirds of its markers.
3. A handful of test points are dropped from sheets they cannot be on: TP13
is a hi-res point and cannot be on sheet 1, TP2 and TP5 are current-section
points and cannot be on sheet 3, TP3 and TP4 likewise on sheet 4.
WHAT IS NOT DONE, and it is the biggest gap in this dataset: no test point has
a hand-placed marker on any sheet. Dropping the legend rows was right, but the
flag symbols on the nets have not been measured to replace them. Until they
are, use the zone reference each test point carries in its source field --
TP1 = INPUT HI (PG1C7) and so on -- which is the legend's own answer and is
printed on the sheet.
LATER PASS. Forty-eight of the surviving 'agreed' markers were rendered and
looked at, chosen where the designator's series suggested it belonged on
another sheet. Twenty-two were wrong -- nineteen are dropped above and three
(U4 on sheet 1, L8 on sheet 3, E2 on sheet 4) are corrected by a hand
placement, which replaces the read without needing a drop. What they sat on:
a pin label (R6, R8 on 'A0'; Q6, Q7 on 'D6'/'D7'; L8 on the pin number '20';
C11 on 'CLR'), a net name or its zone reference (U2 on 'INPUT B', R4 on

'DG444 ON=', RT1/RT2 on 'RST1'/'RST2', C13 on '22mA/220mA OUTPUT'), or blank
space (C5, C70, E2 twice). That is 22 of 48 in the one tier this dataset
trusts -- the pitfalls note's 'a third to a half of a sheet is wrong', met
again on the good tier. Every part that was genuinely drawn somewhere the
reader never looked is hand-placed in 'schematic' below rather than lost.
THIRD PASS. One more 'agreed' marker was found wrong and is dropped here:
U5 on sheet 3 sat on U9's label under the 5801 driver body (U5 is a DG444,
U9 is the UCN5801A that is drawn there). U9 is hand-placed on that label and

(sheetImageSize above), box centre on the printed designator in the circuit
body. A manual entry replaces whatever the reader put on that sheet, so a
designator listed here needs no dropSchematic line.
Thirty-five parts had a board position and no schematic position at all. All
thirty-five are drawn on a sheet and all thirty-five are placed here: each was
found by reading the sheet down at low resolution, searched for with the
image-to-text tools where the reader had nothing, measured off
review_markers.py --grid at full resolution, and rendered back with --proposed
or --refs before being believed. Twenty-three of them the reader had in fact
seen and thrown away with its weak tiers -- C16, C54, C56, C59, C62, HR2, Q4,
all collision, ambiguous or single. The other twelve (C18, C32, C40, C43, C65,
E1, L10, R1, R60, R83, R90, U6) it never read at all.
Twelve further entries replace markers this pass found to be wrong -- see the
note above dropSchematic. Each one's note says what the reader had instead.
HR2 is drawn three times: the dc amplifier and the shunt resistor network on
sheet 1, the heater element on sheet 2. Sheet 1 is placed on the amplifier,
which is what fault codes 2706 and 2707 name; the RNET's coordinates are in
that entry's note. U6 is the same case in miniature -- U6 A is placed because
its output is the CUR/COMP MONITOR at TP9, and U6 B's coordinates are noted.
No test point is hand-placed here yet; that gap is still open.
THIRD PASS. Sixty-one parts had a board position and no schematic position.
Sixty are placed here; only Z4 is not, and Z4 is a parts-list-only row -- it
shares stock number 645341 with Z3, carries no manufacturer part number, and
no 'Z4' is printed on any of the four sheets (searched sheet by sheet).
Twenty-six of the sixty were correct collision reads at the correct pixel:
build_coords discards the collision tier outright, so two designators claiming
one label lose both. Cropping each contested pixel settled which was real --
C10 not C12 on sheet 1 and C12 not C10 on sheet 2, CR11 not CR1, CR12 not
CR10, Q18 not U18, Q10 not Q18/U18, R94 not R54, R20 not R28. Six more of
those crops read a third designator altogether and are recorded as that part:
Q20 where the reader had U20, C60 where it had C68, U10 where it had U18,
R4 where it had Z2, Q15 where it had U15, R63 where it had K5.
The rest were found with the image-to-text tools and measured off a crop.

read PG1C7, PG1D1, PG1A3; sheet 4's is at D1 and its entries read PG4D4,

from the same ink profile the crop rectangles came from: the band is about 60
